strengths: Compelling Multi-modal Integration: The paper tackles the challenging problem of 3D object reconstruction under severe occlusion during in-hand manipulation by elegantly fusing single-view egocentric vision with proprioception (hand geometry) and tactile touch.

Physically Grounded Formulation: It introduces well-designed training objectives and inference-time guidance (contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses) applied directly to a continuous and differentiable camera-aligned SDF representation. The use of decoder-guidance to steer the generative flow-matching model towards physically valid configurations is highly effective.

Rigorous Evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly tested in simulation against strong baselines (Amodal3R and SAM3D), demonstrating superior performance especially in highly occluded scenarios and pose estimation.
Real-world Deployment: The paper shows successful transfer of the model to a real humanoid robot setup with an unseen end-effector, showcasing robustness to cross-embodiment differences.
weaknesses: Resolution Constraints: Representing the 3D scene on a fixed-resolution SDF grid (64^3) limits the capability to capture fine-grained geometries or thin structures, which are common in daily manipulation targets.

Sensitivity to Calibration Noise: The method relies heavily on precise camera-hand extrinsics and forward kinematics. The real-world results show a performance dip (e.g., in F-score) compared to simulation, indicating sensitivity to typical system calibration errors.

Pipeline Complexity: The architecture is quite complex, involving a multi-stage process with a Structure-VAE, a flow-matching transformer, pre-training, fine-tuning with physical losses, and downstream texturing/refinement stages.

strengths: Multimodal Fusion: Integrates vision, proprioception (hand geometry), and multi-contact touch into a single, cohesive 3D generative reconstruction pipeline, addressing severe occlusion in-hand.

Physically Grounded Guidance: Uses non-interpenetration and contact consistency not only as training losses but also as test-time decoder guidance to steer flow-matching sampling toward physically plausible configurations.
Comprehensive Evaluation: Stratifies performance across multiple occlusion bins, clearly demonstrating where touch and proprioception provide the most significant gains (under high occlusion).

Real-world and Cross-embodiment Validation: Successfully demonstrates the method's transferability by deploying it on a real humanoid robot with a hand configuration different from the simulation training data.
weaknesses: Lack of Visual-Tactile Baselines: The evaluation only compares against vision-only baselines (Amodal3R and SAM3D). This proves that adding touch helps, which is intuitive, but fails to benchmark against state-of-the-art visual-tactile reconstruction methods (e.g., TouchSDF or other fusion techniques).

Heavy Reliance on Accurate State Estimation: The system is sensitive to calibration and forward kinematics errors. Since the hand and object share a canonical grid, any drift or error in hand pose directly corrupts the physical guidance, potentially degrading the generation quality.

Assumption of Perfect Input Masks: The method relies on hand and object masks (Mh, Mo) during inference. In real-world manipulation scenarios under severe occlusion, obtaining perfect instance masks is highly challenging and prone to failure.

Low Spatial Resolution: The 3D grid resolution of 64^3 is quite coarse, especially when shared with the hand. This significantly limits the reconstruction of fine-grained geometric features, thin structures, or complex object boundaries.

Simplistic Tactile Encoding: Converting rich tactile sensor readings (e.g., from XELA sensors) into a binary contact grid and Euclidean distance field discards continuous physical signals like force magnitude and contact normals.

strengths: A well-motivated and physically sound formulation that integrates both positive contact evidence (tactile sensors) and negative non-interpenetration constraints (proprioceptive hand geometry) for amodal 3D reconstruction under hand occlusion.

The method uses a camera-aligned, metric SDF representation which allows differentiable physics losses during training and test-time physical guidance (decoder-based optimization) during flow-matching sampling.
The paper provides a comprehensive evaluation in simulation and on a real humanoid robot, showing robust generalization to an unseen end-effector morphology (cross-embodiment transfer).
Writing quality is high; the pipeline is described clearly, and the qualitative results (including trajectory visualization) effectively demonstrate the impact of physical constraints.
weaknesses: The reconstruction resolution of the Structure-VAE is limited to $64^3$, which limits the ability to capture fine-grained geometry and thin features in Stage A.

The evaluation setup for the baseline SAM3D in pose estimation uses ground-truth depth (the 'best-case scenario' for SAM3D), whereas the proposed method does not require depth. While this highlights the strength of the proposed method, the comparison in Tab. 2 could be better contextualized to explain the exact inputs available to each method.

Real-world performance relies heavily on precise hand-camera calibration and forward kinematics. Although the authors analyze tactile noise, a more systematic evaluation of robustness to kinematic calibration errors (joint encoder or camera extrinsics drift) would strengthen the analysis of real-world applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly challenging and important problem at the intersection of computer vision and robotics: reconstructing accurate, metric-scale 3D objects under severe occlusion during manipulation.

Integrating physical constraints (such as contact-consistency and non-interpenetration) directly into both the generative training losses and the inference denoising stage (via decoder-based physics guidance) is elegant and physically sound.
The multi-modal conditioning scheme represents heterogeneous signals (RGB image, masks, hand geometry, and sparse tactile points) in a unified, pose-aware, camera-aligned 3D grid.
The validation is comprehensive, spanning extensive simulation studies, detailed ablations, and physical robot experiments showing successful zero-shot transfer to an unseen robotic hand embodiment.
weaknesses: The method is restricted to a relatively low-resolution voxel grid (64^3), which inherently limits the reconstruction of fine-grained structures, thin parts, and intricate concavities.

There is a strong dependency on high-quality camera-hand calibration and forward kinematics. As shown in the real-world results, small misalignments or noisy proprioception lead to noticeable reconstruction artifacts and surface-hand interpenetrations.
The current inference latency (ranging from 11s to 18s per step) is relatively high, limiting its applicability to real-time closed-loop robotic manipulation tasks.
The tactile feedback is simplified to binary contact grids and Euclidean distance fields. Richer tactile signatures, such as force vectors or continuous pressure distributions, are not utilized.

strengths: Innovative integration of multi-contact tactile sensing, proprioception, and visual cues inside a conditional flow-matching generative model to resolve severe hand-occlusion ambiguities.

The use of physics-derived objectives (non-interpenetration and contact consistency) both as training losses and as decoder-based guidance during sampling effectively ensures physical plausibility of the generated 3D shapes.
Comprehensive validation including simulation (YCB), comparative evaluation on human-hand benchmarks (DexYCB against EasyHOI and FollowMyHold), and real-world deployment on a physical humanoid robot.
Demonstrates robust cross-embodiment generalization, successfully transferring to a real humanoid robot with a hand morphology and tactile sensor layout unseen during training.
Thorough ablation studies verifying the relative contribution of each sensor modality, robustness to various types of input noise (mask, kinematics, tactile), and training/inference components.
weaknesses: High sensitivity to camera-hand calibration and kinematic noise. As shown in the ablation, small calibration errors of 5mm-1cm degrade reconstruction metrics (Voxel IoU drops), posing a challenge for noisy real-world robotic environments.
Resolution limitations: The reliance on a fixed 64^3 grid for the continuous SDF limits the capturing of fine-grained, thin-shell structures or sharp concavities.

Inference latency: While significantly faster than optimization-based baselines, requiring ~8-18 seconds (Stage A + B) on high-end GPUs like RTX A6000/H200 might still be too slow for real-time, closed-loop manipulation tasks.

strengths: A well-motivated and comprehensive framework that integrates egocentric vision, proprioception (posed hand), and multi-contact touch for physically grounded amodal 3D object reconstruction.

Technically sound formulation using a camera-aligned SDF representation (Structure-VAE) and conditional flow matching, enriched with differentiable physics-based objectives (non-interpenetration and contact-consistency) used both during training and as decoder-guidance at inference.
Good generalization demonstrated by deploying the system on a real humanoid robot with a different hand embodiment from the one used in simulation.
Thorough ablation studies verifying the contributions of individual modalities, losses, and robustness to different noise levels (kinematic calibration, masks, tactile).
The paper is very well-written, with clear explanations, neat figures, and comprehensive supplementary material.
weaknesses: The performance gains over the vision-only baseline SAM3D [65] are somewhat modest on certain metrics. For example, in Table 1 and Table 3, SAM3D actually outperforms the proposed method on the F@0.02 metric overall and under low-to-moderate occlusion. Given the high hardware and calibration complexity of the proposed method (tactile sensors, accurate kinematics, calibrated camera-to-hand extrinsics), the practical benefit of these extra modalities over a strong vision-only system is slightly diminished.

High sensitivity to kinematic and calibration noise. As shown in the real-world qualitative results (Fig 4, third row) and the ablation studies (Table 4), the performance degrades noticeably when there is hand-eye calibration or joint encoder noise, which is common in real-robot deployments.
Operating on a fixed-resolution 3D grid of 64^3 limits the geometric fidelity of the reconstructed shapes, especially for thin structures or complex concavities, as also noted by the authors.
